title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Pool and spa servicing
audience: Solo operators and team owners of pool and spa servicing businesses who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their route.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list that is scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a pool need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. Write down the pool types you service well, such as residential fortnightly pools, holiday-let pools and spas, the price range you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs you. A fortnightly round on a route you already run is worth far more to a small business than a single large repair across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows.

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, using the written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who decides, and whether the work falls within the licence and insurance you hold. Holiday-let managers, real estate agencies that sell homes with pools, body corporate or owners corporation committees, and aquatic centres run by councils or schools are examples of prospects to score. Add a prospect only when it passes the criteria. Business.gov.au suggests a short profile for each segment (24 September 2024). Confirm the scope, your capacity and the deadline before you send a quote (Business Queensland, 16 November 2022). Keep only business contact details that are published for business use. Do not use bought or harvested contact lists, because buying a list does not remove the need to show consent (ACMA, Spam Act obligations, 28 March 2019).

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a pool need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a need more likely soon. Examples for pools include a holiday-letting business adding a property with a pool to its listings, a new fit-out or refurbishment at a body corporate or a holiday complex, and a pool that a business has just put up for sale or lease. Use signals to decide when to make contact, not to build a profile of individuals. Do not monitor private people, do not use personal information that is not public, and do not turn up at a home to make an offer. Public tender registers are useful signals about public bodies. In Victoria, Buying for Victoria lists current and past tenders, and suppliers can set alerts (last updated 7 August 2026). Some councils publish planning permit registers with suburb and status fields, such as the City of Casey register on the Victorian open-data portal, so check whether your own council publishes one. The research did not find a public list of pools due for barrier inspection, so do not assume one exists.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message does three things. It says how you came to know about the business or the work. It makes one specific observation that you can check from public view or from the business's own published material, such as a listing that shows a pool with no pool service named on it. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined set of pools or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found many approaches were pressured or misleading, and many salespeople did not identify themselves (28 July 2026). A specific, honest message that names you is therefore a practical advantage as well as a compliance step.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, followed by a pause. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work, and move your effort toward them.

procedure: Write the pool type, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules, the do-not-call rules for any call, and the licence rules for the work before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A pool business covers three suburbs. A holiday-letting business publishes a new listing for a house with a pool in one of them, and its general enquiries email address is on its website. A public notice also goes up about planned works at a body corporate building in the same suburb.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the owner send a sales message to the holiday-letting business now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The owner should not send a sales email just because a business address is published. ACMA's Spam Act guidance says publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages, so the owner first checks whether the business has agreed to receive them or has invited contact. If neither applies, the owner waits for an invitation or uses a route the business has agreed to. A phone call to a registered number is limited by the Do Not Call Register rules, so the owner checks the register before calling. Any message that does go out names the listing, says how the business learned of it, offers one specific item the owner could handle, such as a barrier check before the next booking season, and asks one question. The owner does not contact the body corporate's individual owners or tenants using any private details, and does not enter the common area without an invitation.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, pool type and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual homeowner to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Offering a barrier certificate or a licensed service that you are not licensed or insured to deliver in that state.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the licence and insurance for each state before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a licensed or authorised pool service in outreach unless you hold the licence that the state where the work is done requires. Pool barrier inspections and certificates are issued by registered inspectors in Victoria, and by QBCC-licensed pool safety inspectors in Queensland. A pool service business should not offer or describe a certificate in any state unless the state's rule allows it. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days (read 2026-11-03). ACMA's Spam Act obligations page (last updated 28 March 2019) says publishing an address does not by itself permit commercial messages. The Act text was not read for this lesson.

Information on a public listing or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, the OAIC's guidance on direct marketing (APP 7, version dated 22 July 2019) says that public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

Telemarketing to registered numbers is limited by the Do Not Call Register rules, which the DNCR industry guide (2018 copyright notice, older) describes as weekdays from 9 am to 8 pm and Saturdays from 9 am to 5 pm. Check the register before any call.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the pool work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should a pool business contact first?
options: A one-off pool a long way outside your service area, because it looks large
A holiday-letting business with several pools inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on services

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned works at a body corporate building in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the building's manager about the works, by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each owner using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for your pool service
Go into the common area to look at the pool before making contact and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and it has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first and then send the message
Confirm the Spam Act 2003 requirements in current ACMA guidance before sending

sourceReferences: ACMA, 'Avoid sending spam', https://www.acma.gov.au/avoid-sending-spam, no date shown; read 2026-11-03. Supports: marketing messages need consent, which must be recorded; unsubscribe honoured within five working days. The Spam Act 2003 (Cth) text was not read; check it before sending.

ACMA, 'Spam Act obligations', https://www.acma.gov.au/theACMA/spam-industry-obligations, last updated 28 March 2019 (older source). Supports: publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages; buying a list does not remove the need to prove consent.

OAIC, 'Chapter 7: APP 7 direct marketing', https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles/australian-privacy-principles-guidelines/chapter-7-app-7-direct-marketing, page modified 16 October 2023; version 1.1 dated 22 July 2019 (older). Supports: public information is not exempt from direct-marketing rules.

OAIC, 'Australian Privacy Principles guidelines', https://www.oaic.gov.au/privacy/australian-privacy-principles-guidelines/, published and updated 13 May 2026. Supports: the Act covers organisations above a turnover threshold and some others; small-business coverage is unconfirmed here.
business.gov.au, 'How to identify your target market', https://business.gov.au/marketing/how-to-identify-your-target-market, 24 September 2024. Supports: one short profile for each segment.

Business Queensland, 'Preparing a business quote: tips', https://www.business.qld.gov.au/running-business/marketing-sales/sales/preparing-quote/tips, last updated 16 November 2022. Supports: clarify the work, your capacity and deadlines before quoting.

Buying for Victoria, 'How to get known', https://buyingfor.vic.gov.au/how-get-known, last updated 7 August 2026. Victoria. Supports: current and past tenders are listed, suppliers can set alerts, and agencies publish annual procurement plans.

DataVic, 'Planning Permit Application Register' (City of Casey), https://discover.data.vic.gov.au/dataset/planning-permit-application-register, metadata published 15 November 2023, last updated 5 November 2026 as shown. Example of a council register; check your own council.

ACCC, 'Misleading and high pressure unsolicited sales practices widespread', https://www.accc.gov.au/media-release/misleading-and-high-pressure-unsolicited-sales-practices-widespread, 28 July 2026. Supports: many approaches were pressured or misleading; about 71% of salespeople identified themselves.

Do Not Call Register, 'DNCR industry guide', https://www.donotcall.gov.au/media/1212/dncr-industry-guide.pdf, 2018 copyright notice (older). Supports: telemarketing hours for registered numbers; lists must be washed against the register.

Building and Plumbing Commission, 'Swimming pools and spas', https://www.bpc.vic.gov.au/home-owners/home-renovation-and-building-essentials/swimming-pools-and-spas, last updated 30 June 2026. Victoria. Supports: owners must use a registered inspector, building inspector or building surveyor for the four-year inspection.

QBCC, 'Pool safety inspector', https://www.qbcc.qld.gov.au/home-building-owners/pool-safety/find-pool-safety-inspector-search-property-psi-login, dated 31 August 2021. Queensland. Supports: pool safety inspectors are licensed by the QBCC and issue certificates or non-conformity notices.

Gap: no pool-specific prospect or referral-source figure was found. The research did not confirm a pool trade-body or aquatic-centre tender source. Public lists of pools due for barrier inspection were not found.

officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: marketing messages need consent, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include correct contact details; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option honoured within five working days. Does not cover privacy law. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Australian Privacy Principles guidelines (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-03: the APPs apply to organisations covered by the Privacy Act, which the page says covers organisations with an annual turnover of more than $3 million and some other organisations. Small-business coverage and consent detail are unconfirmed here. Publisher: OAIC.
